lessons.title: Wool Growth and Fiber Characteristics
lessons.body:
Wool grows from follicles in the sheep's skin. Each follicle produces a single fiber. The number of follicles varies by breed: Merino sheep have up to 100 follicles per square millimeter, while indigenous African breeds like the Namaqua Afrikaner may have only 20â30. More follicles mean denser fleece. Wool grows continuously; a Merino can produce 4â6 kg of fleece per year, while local breeds yield 1â2 kg. Growth rate depends on nutrition, genetics, and season. In Africa, sheep on poor grazing may grow only 1 cm per month, while well-fed sheep can grow 2â3 cm.

Fiber characteristics determine wool quality. Fiber diameter (measured in microns) is the most important: fine wool (under 24 microns) is soft and used for clothing; medium (24â31 microns) for blankets; coarse (over 31 microns) for carpets. Crimp (natural waviness) gives wool elasticity. Staple length is the length of fibers in one year's growth; longer staples (7â12 cm) are easier to spin. Clean wool yield is the percentage of wool left after removing grease, dirt, and vegetable matter. African sheep often have high grease content, so yield may be 50â70%.

Breed choice matters. Merino, Rambouillet, and their crosses produce fine wool but need good management. Indigenous breeds like the Blackhead Persian have carpet-type wool but are hardy. For African smallholders, crossbreeding local ewes with Merino rams can improve wool while keeping hardiness. Wool color is usually white, but some breeds produce black, brown, or spotted fleeces; these are harder to dye and fetch lower prices.

To improve wool growth: provide balanced nutrition, especially protein and sulfur-containing amino acids. Avoid stresses like parasites and extreme heat. Shearing once or twice a year prevents fleece from matting and allows staple length measurement. Keep records of fleece weight and quality to select best animals. Remember: wool is a renewable resourceâhealthy sheep produce good wool year after year.

lessons.title: Shearing Techniques and Timing
lessons.body:
Shearing is removing the fleece in one piece. It requires sharp hand shears or electric clippers. For small flocks, hand shears are common in Africa; they cost less and need no power. Electric clippers are faster but require electricity or a generator. Before shearing, gather: sharp shears, a clean tarp, a rope or shearing stand, and a first-aid kit. Do not shear wet sheepâwool must be dry to avoid rot and to get a good price.

Timing is critical. In most African regions, shear once a year, just before the rainy season. This prevents fleece from getting soaked and dirty, and allows sheep to grow a new coat before cold or wet weather. In hot, dry areas, shear twice: early spring and late summer. Avoid shearing in late pregnancy (stress can cause abortion) or during extreme cold. Lambs can be shorn at 6â8 months for the first time.

Technique: Restrain the sheep by sitting it on its rump, holding it between your legs. Start at the belly and crutch (between hind legs), then the legs, then the sides, and finally the back. Use long, smooth strokes close to the skin, but avoid cutting the skin. Change shears or sharpen every 10â15 minutes. A skilled shearer can do a sheep in 3â5 minutes with clippers, or 10â15 minutes with hand shears. Keep the fleece in one pieceâit's called a

and is easier to class and skirt.

After shearing, treat any cuts with antiseptic. Keep the sheep in a clean, dry pen for a few hours. The fleece should be rolled: spread it on a clean tarp, remove dirty edges (skirting), then roll from the back to the belly, tying with paper twine. Store in a dry, ventilated place away from rodents. Never use plastic bagsâthey trap moisture and cause mold. Shearing is also a health check: look for wounds, ticks, and lumps. Record fleece weight and any issues. Good shearing increases wool value and keeps sheep healthy.

lessons.title: Wool Handling and Classing
lessons.body:
After shearing, wool must be handled carefully to maintain quality. Classing is sorting fleeces into uniform groups based on fiber diameter, staple length, color, and cleanliness. This allows you to sell wool at better prices because buyers want consistent lots. For small flocks, classing can be done on a clean table or tarp.

First, skirt the fleece: remove all dirty, stained, and short fibers from the edges (belly, crutch, and legs). These are called

and are sold separately at low prices. Then assess the fleece. Key criteria: fiber diameter (use a micrometer or visual appraisal), staple length (measure with a ruler), crimp (fine wool has more crimp), and color (white is best). Also check for vegetable matter (grass seeds, burrs) and stains (from urine, dung, or branding).

Class into grades. Common grades for African wool: Fine (under 24 microns) â for apparel; Medium (24â31 microns) â for blankets and sweaters; Coarse (over 31 microns) â for carpets and rugs. In some markets, you may also class by breed or by fleece part (e.g., shoulders are best). Keep each grade separate in clean burlap bags or wool packs. Label each bag with grade, weight, and date. Never mix gradesâit reduces the value of the entire lot.

For small-scale farmers, classing may be as simple as three piles: good, medium, and poor. But even this improves returns. If you have many sheep, consider a wool classer course or work with a cooperative. Remember: clean wool is worth more. Remove as much dirt as possible before classing. Store bags on pallets in a dry, dark room. Avoid contamination from oil, chemicals, or animal hair. Good classing shows buyers you are professional and can lead to repeat sales and higher prices.

lessons.title: Skirting and Packaging
lessons.body:
Skirting is the process of removing the edges of the fleece that are dirty, stained, or of low quality. It is done immediately after shearing, before the fleece is rolled. Skirting increases the value of the main fleece by removing contaminants. On a clean tarp, spread the fleece with the cut side down. The belly, crutch, and leg areas are usually the dirtiest. Also remove any short fibers from the neck and head. Use your hands or shears to pull away these parts. The skirtings can be sold separately for low-grade products like felt or insulation.

After skirting, the fleece is rolled. Start from the back (the cleanest part) and roll toward the belly, keeping the fleece compact. Tie the roll with paper twine or a similar biodegradable material. Do not use plastic baler twineâit contaminates wool during processing. For packaging, use clean burlap bags or woven polypropylene wool packs. These allow air circulation. Never use plastic bags, as they trap moisture and cause mold. Each pack should weigh 100â150 kg for easy handling, but smallholders can use smaller bags of 20â50 kg.

Label each pack clearly: your name, farm, date, grade, and weight. If you have multiple grades, use separate packs. Store packs in a dry, well-ventilated shed on wooden pallets, away from walls. Protect from rodents, insects, and moisture. In humid regions, use a dehumidifier or place bags on raised platforms. Check regularly for signs of mold or pests. If you sell to a cooperative or trader, they may have specific packaging requirementsâask first.

Proper skirting and packaging prevent downgrading and reduce weight loss. A well-packed fleece can fetch 10â20% more than a poorly handled one. For African farmers, simple improvements like using clean burlap bags and tying with paper twine make a big difference. Remember: buyers judge wool by its presentation. Clean, well-labeled packs show you are serious and can lead to better prices and long-term relationships.

lessons.title: Wool Marketing
lessons.body:
Wool marketing involves selling your wool for the best possible price. In Africa, options include selling to local traders, cooperatives, or through auctions. Each has pros and cons. Local traders offer immediate cash but often pay low prices. Cooperatives pool wool from many farmers to get better prices and access to larger buyers. Auctions, like those in South Africa (e.g., Port Elizabeth), require grading and volume but can fetch premium prices. For smallholders, cooperatives are often the best route.

Before selling, know your wool's value. Factors: fiber diameter (finer is better), staple length (longer is better), cleanliness (low vegetable matter), and color (white is best). Get a sample tested if possibleâmany agricultural extension offices offer this. Current market prices vary: in 2023, fine Merino wool in South Africa sold for around R150âR200 per kg, while coarse wool sold for R50âR80 per kg. In East Africa, prices are lower, but demand for carpet wool is growing.

To market effectively: join or form a cooperative. Pool your wool with neighbors to meet minimum volumes (often 500 kg or more). Grade and class your wool properlyâbuyers pay more for uniform lots. Build relationships with buyers: attend agricultural shows, contact wool brokers, and ask for feedback. Consider value addition: some farmers sell washed or carded wool for hand-spinning, which can double the price. But this requires extra labor and equipment.

Timing matters. Wool prices fluctuate with global demand. Avoid selling immediately after shearing when markets are flooded. Store wool properly and sell when prices are higher. Keep records of sales, prices, and buyer contacts. Use the money to reinvest in your flockâbetter rams, feed, or shearing equipment. Remember: marketing is not just selling; it's understanding what buyers want and delivering it consistently. With good quality and reliable supply, you can build a reputation and get better prices year after year.

lessons.title: Record Keeping for Wool Production
lessons.body:
Record keeping is essential for improving wool production and profitability. Without records, you cannot know which sheep produce the best wool, how much you harvest, or where you can improve. Start simple: a notebook or a spreadsheet on a phone. Record each shearing event, fleece weight, grade, and any health issues. Also record feed, treatments, and breeding dates.

For each sheep, keep an individual record: ear tag number, breed, date of birth, and fleece weight at each shearing. Note fiber diameter if tested, staple length, and any defects (e.g., tender fleece, stains). This helps you select replacement ewes and rams. Cull sheep that consistently produce poor wool. Over time, you can increase average fleece weight and quality.

At the flock level, record total wool produced per year, average fleece weight, and income from sales. Calculate cost of production: feed, labor, shearing, packaging, and transport. This tells you if wool is profitable. For example, if you produce 100 kg of wool and sell at R100 per kg, income is R10,000. If costs are R6,000, profit is R4,000. Compare across years to see trends.

Use records for decision-making. If a certain breed or cross performs better, expand it. If a particular season gives lower fleece weight, adjust nutrition. If a buyer pays more for a certain grade, focus on producing that grade. Records also help when applying for loans or grantsâthey show you are a serious farmer. In Africa, mobile apps like FarmBook or simple Excel sheets can help. Share records with your cooperative or extension officer for advice. Remember: what gets measured gets managed. Good records lead to better wool and more money.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Wool Production and Management

This practical reference consolidates the core operational knowledge a sheep farmer, wool handler or agribusiness manager needs to produce, prepare and sell wool profitably in an African context. It is written for commercial and emerging producers who want to move from "selling whatever comes off the sheep" to a disciplined, quality-driven wool enterprise. Wool is a renewable, high-value fibre, but its price at the farm gate is determined long before the shearer arrives: genetics, nutrition, health, shearing timing, skirting, classing, packaging and record keeping all feed into the final cheque. Treat this module as your operating manual.

Why Wool Matters Commercially in Africa

Africa produces wool across a wide range of climates and systems. South Africa is the continent's dominant commercial wool producer, with the Eastern Cape, Free State and Karoo regions supplying Merino and Dohne Merino wool to global markets. Lesotho, Namibia, Kenya, Tanzania, Ethiopia and Morocco also produce wool, often from indigenous or crossbred flocks. The global wool market pays premiums for clean, well-classed, low-contamination fleece, which means smallholder and commercial producers alike can capture value by improving preparation. Wool also hedges against drought: it can be stored, does not spoil like meat or milk, and can be sold when prices are favourable.

Wool Growth and Fibre Characteristics: What You Are Selling

Wool is a protein fibre (keratin) grown from follicles in the skin. Three characteristics determine its commercial value: fibre diameter (micron), staple length, and style/cleanliness. Fibre diameter is the single biggest price driver. Merino wool in the 18â22 micron range commands strong premiums for apparel; 23â28 micron goes into knitwear and upholstery; above 30 micron is typically used in carpets and interior textiles. Staple length affects processing: longer staples (75 mm+) suit worsted spinning, shorter staples suit woollens. Cleanliness â freedom from dust, vegetable matter, urine stain and polypropylene contamination â determines yield after scouring.

Nutrition drives wool growth more than genetics in the short term. Protein (especially sulphur-containing amino acids), energy and trace minerals (zinc, copper, selenium) directly affect fibre diameter and tensile strength. A sudden nutritional stress can produce a "break" in the staple, reducing its value. Wool growth is also seasonal: in most African environments, wool grows fastest in the warm, well-fed months and slows in winter or dry season. Plan shearing and marketing around this cycle.

Shearing Techniques and Timing

Shearing is a skilled, welfare-critical operation. In South Africa, most flocks are shorn once or twice a year, typically in spring (AugustâOctober) and sometimes again in autumn. Timing depends on: (1) avoiding cold stress on freshly shorn animals, (2) wool length (too long risks cotting and contamination; too short reduces value), and (3) market timing. Shearers should be trained and accredited; the standard is the "New Zealand" or "Bowen" technique, which uses long, smooth blows close to the skin to maximise staple length and minimise second cuts. Second cuts (short fibres) reduce classing value.

Before shearing: keep sheep dry (wet wool stains and can rot), withhold feed for 12 hours to reduce stress and contamination, and set up a clean, flat, well-lit board. Use sharp, well-oiled gear. After shearing, keep fleece intact and throw it onto a clean table â never the floor. Tag each fleece with the animal's ID if you are recording performance.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Shearing and Handling

  • Never shear wet sheep. Wet wool cannot be classed or sold at full value, and wet fleeces can heat, rot and spontaneously combust in storage.
  • Use proper restraint. Shearers suffer back, wrist and cut injuries. Use a shearing cradle or upright restraint; never wrestle a sheep on the ground.
  • Keep first-aid on hand. Shearing cuts are common â have antiseptic, bandages and a tetanus-aware protocol. Sheep can also kick and cause serious injury.
  • Protect against zoonoses. Wear gloves and boots; wash hands after handling. Sheep can carry orf, ringworm and other infections transmissible to humans.
  • Manage heat and dust. Shearing sheds in hot African summers can exceed 40Â°C. Provide shade, water and rest breaks for workers.

Wool Handling, Classing, Skirting and Packaging

Skirting is the first quality step: remove the belly wool, crutchings, dags, stained pieces and any fleece with vegetable matter or polypropylene contamination. The main fleece (the "skirted fleece") is then classed. Classing separates wool into uniform lines by micron, staple length, strength, colour and style. On commercial farms, classers work to a line specification; on smaller farms, classing may be done at the cooperative or auction floor. Key rules: never mix fleece types in one bale; never include stained or contaminated wool; and always label bales with the line, farm, classer and date.

Packaging protects the value you have created. Use clean, dry, UV-resistant wool packs (jute or approved synthetic). Press bales to standard density (typically around 200 kg for a standard wool bale in South Africa). Store on pallets in a dry, ventilated, rodent-free shed, off the floor and away from chemicals, fuel and fertiliser. Contamination from polypropylene, hay twine, or chemical odours is one of the most common causes of price penalties.

Wool Marketing and Record Keeping

Wool is sold through three main channels in Africa: (1) auction â the dominant route in South Africa, where brokers present bales to buyers; (2) direct contract â selling to a processor or exporter at a negotiated price; and (3) cooperative or local market â common for smallholders, often at lower prices but with lower transaction costs. To capture value, you need objective measurement: a sample tested for micron, yield and vegetable matter content. Cape Wools SA and SGS provide testing services. Without a test, buyers discount your wool because they assume the worst.

Record keeping is the backbone of improvement. For every fleece or bale, record: animal ID (if individual), class/line, greasy weight, test result (micron, yield), date, buyer and price. Over time, this data lets you identify which bloodlines, nutrition programs and shearing times produce the best returns. It also supports credit applications and cooperative negotiations. Use a simple spreadsheet or a farm management app; the key is consistency, not complexity.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Shear dry sheep only. Wet wool loses value and can rot or combust in storage.
  • Keep the board and packs clean. One strand of polypropylene can downgrade a whole bale.
  • Skirt first, class second, bale last. Never mix belly wool, stains or dags with the main fleece.
  • Label every bale with line, farm, classer and date â traceability builds buyer trust.
  • Test a sample for micron

quiz.q: What is the main factor that determines wool quality?
quiz.explanation: Fiber diameter (micron) is the most important factor affecting wool softness and end use.

quiz.q: How many kilograms of fleece can a Merino sheep produce per year?
quiz.explanation: Merino sheep are known for high fleece weight, typically 4-6 kg per year.

quiz.q: Which breed is known for fine wool?
quiz.explanation: Merino sheep are famous for producing fine wool under 24 microns.

quiz.q: What does 'clean wool yield' refer to?
options: A) The weight of wool after shearing
B) The percentage of wool left after removing impurities
C) The length of the staple
D) The number of crimps per inch
quiz.explanation: Clean wool yield is the proportion of usable wool after removing grease, dirt, and vegetable matter.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid shearing sheep when they are wet?
options: A) It is harder to cut
B) The wool may rot and get lower price
C) The sheep may get pneumonia
quiz.explanation: Wet wool can develop mold and rot, reducing its value and quality.

quiz.q: What is the best time to shear sheep in most African regions?
options: A) Just before the rainy season
B) In the middle of the dry season
quiz.explanation: Shearing before the rains prevents fleece from getting soaked and dirty.

quiz.q: Which tool is commonly used for shearing in small-scale African farms?
quiz.explanation: Hand shears are affordable and do not require electricity, making them common for small flocks.

quiz.q: What is the first step in shearing a sheep?
options: B) Start at the belly and crutch
quiz.explanation: Shearing typically begins at the belly and crutch to remove dirty wool first.

quiz.q: What should you do with a fleece immediately after shearing?
options: B) Roll it and tie with paper twine
C) Store in a plastic bag
quiz.explanation: Rolling and tying with paper twine keeps the fleece intact and prevents contamination.

quiz.q: What is skirting?
options: A) Removing dirty edges from the fleece
quiz.explanation: Skirting is the removal of stained, dirty, and low-quality edges from the fleece.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a sign of high-quality wool?
quiz.explanation: Uniform color and crimp indicate good quality and consistency.

quiz.q: What is the recommended weight for a wool pack for easy handling?
quiz.explanation: Standard wool packs are 100-150 kg for efficient handling and transport.

quiz.q: Why should you not use plastic bags to store wool?
options: B) They trap moisture and cause mold
D) They are not strong enough
quiz.explanation: Plastic bags prevent air circulation, leading to moisture buildup and mold.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of joining a wool cooperative?
options: B) Access to better prices and larger buyers
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives pool wool to meet volume requirements and negotiate better prices.

quiz.q: Which factor is NOT used in wool classing?
quiz.explanation: Sheep age is not a direct criterion for classing wool; fiber characteristics are used.

quiz.q: What is the approximate price range for fine Merino wool in South Africa in 2023?
quiz.explanation: Fine Merino wool fetched around R150-R200 per kg in 2023.

quiz.q: What is value addition in wool marketing?
options: A) Selling wool immediately after shearing
B) Processing wool into yarn or felt
quiz.explanation: Value addition involves processing wool into higher-value products like yarn or felt.

quiz.q: Why is record keeping important for wool production?
options: B) To identify best performing sheep and make decisions
quiz.explanation: Records help track performance, profitability, and guide management decisions.

quiz.q: What should you record for each sheep at shearing?
quiz.explanation: Fleece weight and grade are key for selecting and culling decisions.

quiz.q: How can records help with loan applications?
options: A) They show you are a serious farmer
quiz.explanation: Good records demonstrate professionalism and financial responsibility to lenders.

quiz.q: What is the recommended storage for wool packs?
options: A) On the floor in a shed
B) On wooden pallets in a dry, ventilated room
quiz.explanation: Pallets and dry, ventilated storage prevent moisture and pest damage.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common defect in wool?
quiz.explanation: Tender fleece breaks easily and reduces wool value.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of tying a fleece with paper twine?
options: A) To make it look neat
B) To prevent contamination from plastic
quiz.explanation: Paper twine is biodegradable and does not contaminate wool during processing.

quiz.q: How often should you shear sheep in hot, dry areas?
quiz.explanation: In hot, dry areas, shearing twice a year (spring and late summer) is recommended.

quiz.q: What is the first step in wool handling after shearing?
quiz.explanation: Skirting removes dirty edges before further handling.

quiz.q: Which grade of wool is used for carpets?
quiz.explanation: Coarse wool (over 31 microns) is used for carpets and rugs.

quiz.q: What is the advantage of selling through an auction?
quiz.explanation: Auctions can fetch higher prices if wool is well-graded and in demand.

quiz.q: What does a high clean wool yield indicate?
options: B) More usable wool after processing
quiz.explanation: High yield means a greater proportion of clean wool, which is more valuable.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid shearing in late pregnancy?
options: C) The wool is too short
D) The shears may cut the lamb
quiz.explanation: Shearing stress can lead to abortion in late pregnancy.

quiz.q: What is the recommended number of follicles per square millimeter for fine wool breeds like Merino?
quiz.explanation: Merino sheep can have up to 100 follicles per square millimeter, producing dense fleece.
